items.title: 5.2 A Linear Equation in Two Variables Represents a Straight Line

source_refs.note: Book p. 142: 5.2 Theorem 1 with proof, Case-I (a = 0), Case-II (b = 0), Case-III (a, b non-zero)

blocks.text: Theorem 1: The linear equation \(ax + by + c = 0\) in two variables \(x\) and \(y\) represents a straight line, where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are real numbers and \(a\) and \(b\) are not simultaneously zero.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: What does 'represents a straight line' mean? Collect all the points \((x, y)\) whose coordinates satisfy the equation and plot them. The theorem says these points always form a straight line. The plan of the proof: since \(a\) and \(b\) cannot both be zero, there are only three possibilities (\(a = 0\); \(b = 0\); neither is zero). In each case we rewrite the equation in a form we already know is a line.
Proof: Here, \(a\) and \(b\) cannot be both zero. So, the following cases arise:

Then \(ax + by + c = 0\) becomes
\[by + c = 0\]
or
\[y = -\dfrac{c}{b}\]
which is an equation of the straight line parallel to x-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why may we divide by \(b\)? Because \(a = 0\) and \(a\), \(b\) are not both zero, so \(b \neq 0\). The equation \(y = -\frac{c}{b}\) says that \(y\) has the same value at every point, whatever \(x\) is: a horizontal line at height \(-\frac{c}{b}\).

Then \(ax + by + c = 0\) becomes
\[ax + c = 0\]
or
\[x = -\dfrac{c}{a}\]
which is an equation of straight line parallel to y-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here \(b = 0\), so \(a \neq 0\) and we may divide by \(a\). Every point of \(x = -\frac{c}{a}\) has the same x-coordinate: a vertical line. A vertical line has no slope (it is undefined), which is why it needs its own case.

Then \(ax + by + c = 0\) takes the form
\[by = -ax - c\]
or
\[y = -\dfrac{a}{b}x - \dfrac{c}{b}\]
\[y = mx + k\]
which is slope-intercept form of the straight line with slope \(-\frac{a}{b}\) and y-intercept \(-\frac{c}{b}\).
Thus, equation \(ax + by + c = 0\) always represents a straight line.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The converse is also true: every straight line has an equation of the form \(ax + by + c = 0\).
A vertical line \(x = h\) is \(1x + 0y - h = 0\).
Any other line has a slope \(m\) and a y-intercept \(k\), so \(y = mx + k\), that is \(mx - y + k = 0\).
So 'linear equation in \(x\) and \(y\)' and 'straight line' mean the same thing. That is why such equations are called linear.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration of the three cases:
\(0x + 3y - 12 = 0\) gives \(y = 4\): horizontal line (Case-I).
\(2x + 0y + 6 = 0\) gives \(x = -3\): vertical line (Case-II).
\(2x - 3y + 6 = 0\) gives \(y = \frac{2}{3}x + 2\): slope \(\frac{2}{3}\), y-intercept 2 (Case-III).
Quick rule for Case-III: slope \(= -\frac{a}{b} = -\frac{\text{coefficient of } x}{\text{coefficient of } y}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Every linear equation \(ax + by + c = 0\) (\(a\), \(b\) not both zero) is a straight line, and every straight line has such an equation.
2. \(a = 0\): horizontal line \(y = -\frac{c}{b}\). \(b = 0\): vertical line \(x = -\frac{c}{a}\).
3. \(a \neq 0\), \(b \neq 0\): slope \(-\frac{a}{b}\), y-intercept \(-\frac{c}{b}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the slope as \(\frac{a}{b}\) or \(-\frac{b}{a}\). It is \(-\frac{a}{b}\): solve for \(y\) if unsure.
2. Calling \(y = -\frac{c}{b}\) parallel to the y-axis. \(y\) = constant is horizontal (parallel to the x-axis).
3. Dividing by \(a\) or \(b\) without checking that it is not zero.
